tagline: Where granite peaks vanish into seas of cloud and Ming-dynasty villages sleep in the valleys below.
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for almost everything — set up mobile payment before arrival and carry some cash as backup

taxi.fareNote: Insist on the meter; airport and Tangkou (mountain base) drivers often push flat 'special' fares — agree a price upfront if they refuse to use it

emergency.medical: 120 (ambulance); Huangshan Second People's Hospital in Tunxi
emergency.note: Mountain rescue teams patrol Huangshan's main trails; English is rare on emergency lines — have a Mandarin speaker or your hotel call for you

walk: Tunxi's Old Street and riverside areas are very walkable; the mountain itself demands serious hiking or cable cars, and the ancient villages are best explored on foot along cobblestone lanes

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers, including women; petty crime is rare
safety.crime: Low — occasional overcharging by unlicensed taxis or tour touts near the mountain entrance is the main annoyance

hood_landmark.Tunxi Old Street: Zhen Hai Bridge and the Ming-Qing shopping street
hood_landmark.Huangshan Scenic Area: Mount Huangshan's granite peaks and Sea of Clouds
hood_landmark.Hongcun & Xidi Ancient Villages: Hongcun's Moon Pond and South Lake

hood_desc: A pedestrian Ming-and-Qing-dynasty street of black-tile, white-wall shophouses selling Huizhou ink, tea, and carved inkstones — the city's most walkable, central base.
The granite spine of Mount Huangshan itself — pine-clad peaks, cloud seas, and sunrise views reached by cable car or a punishing stone-step climb from Tangkou village.
Twin UNESCO-listed Huizhou villages of whitewashed courtyard homes reflected in ox-shaped ponds, a short bus ride from Tunxi.
The old Huizhou prefectural capital, its stone memorial archways and Doushan Street preserving 500 years of merchant-clan history.
A quieter Taoist sacred mountain south of the city, its cliffside temples and grottoes drawing far fewer crowds than Huangshan itself.

transit.sys: City buses (Huangshan Bus Group) plus scenic-area shuttle buses
transit.pay: Cash or QR code (WeChat/Alipay) on buses; no unified transit card for tourists
transit.map: Routes aren't on Google/Apple Maps — use Baidu Maps or Amap (Gaode)
transit.note: Most sights outside Tunxi require taxis, Didi, or tour buses; there is no rail/metro system in the city

transport.air: Huangshan Tunxi International Airport (TXN), ~7 km from Tunxi, with flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, and other major Chinese cities
transport.train: Huangshan North railway station sits on the Hefei–Fuzhou and Shanghai–Kunming high-speed lines — about 3 hrs from Shanghai, 1.5 hrs from Hangzhou
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Huangshan to Hangzhou, Shanghai, and Nanjing; local buses run from Tunxi to Tangkou (mountain base) and the ancient villages
transport.ferry: None — Huangshan is inland with no scheduled passenger ferry service
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired car is common for reaching Hongcun, Xidi, and Shexian; roads are good but mountain-area driving and parking get congested in peak season

airport.name: Huangshan Tunxi International Airport
airport.transport: Taxi ~$8-10 metered fare into town; airport shuttle bus to central Tunxi also available

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage in Tunxi and along main roads; patchy on remote mountain trails
net.w: Free wifi in most hotels and cafes, though speeds vary
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.gb: ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM
net.fwn: The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM at Shanghai/Hangzhou airport before onward travel; Tunxi Airport's counter has limited stock

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

tagline: Misty tea mountains and a bamboo raft down the Nine-Bend River, where Da Hong Pao legends grow on sheer red cliffs.
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside a few international-standard hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay dominate — set up mobile payment before arrival and keep some cash as backup

taxi.fareNote: Few taxis circulate — Didi is more reliable than street-hailing, especially near the scenic area entrance

emergency.note: Scenic-area staff carry radios for trail emergencies; English support is minimal — keep your hotel's number handy

visit: Da Hong Pao mother tea bushes
Han-dynasty Min Yue King City ruins, Chengcun
Wuyi Square and Wuyishan City Museum
walk: The scenic core is a trail-and-raft park, not a walkable city grid — you shuttle between trailheads by park bus, then hike; the low-rise city center itself is compact and easy on foot

safety.safety: Very safe, low crime, a popular domestic tea-tourism and honeymoon destination
safety.crime: Minimal — the main risk is overpaying unlicensed drivers or high-pressure tea-tasting sales pitches

hood_landmark.Wuyi Mountain Scenic Area: Tianyou Peak and the Nine-Bend River
hood_landmark.Xingcun: The original Da Hong Pao mother tea bushes
hood_landmark.Xiamei Ancient Village: Zou Family Grand House and the Meixi Canal

hood_desc: The UNESCO core of red sandstone peaks and the Nine-Bend River, explored by bamboo raft and cliffside trail up to Tianyou Peak.
The modern town of Wuyi Avenue and Wuyi Square, home to the region's transit hubs, restaurants, and tea shops.
A working tea-trading town at the scenic area's southern gate, home to the original Da Hong Pao mother bushes and rows of tea-tasting houses.
Site of the 2,000-year-old Min Yue Kingdom's walled capital ruins, plus the region's biggest wholesale tea market.
A canal-laced Qing-dynasty merchant village of carved courtyard houses a short drive from town, far off the main tour-bus route.

transit.sys: Local buses plus a free electric scenic shuttle/tram inside Wuyishan National Park
transit.pay: Cash or QR code; the scenic-area multi-day pass includes shuttle rides
transit.map: Use Amap (Gaode) or Baidu Maps and download offline
transit.note: The park shuttle bus is included in the scenic-area entrance ticket and is the main way to reach trailheads

transport.air: Wuyishan Airport (WUS), ~8 km from the city, with domestic flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, Xiamen, and other major cities
transport.train: Wuyishan East and Wuyishan-Beibus high-speed stations on the Hefei–Fuzhou and Nanping–Wuyishan lines — about 6 hrs from Shanghai, 3-4 hrs from Fuzhou or Xiamen
transport.bus: Regional buses link Wuyishan to Nanping, Fuzhou, and Jiangxi's Shangrao; local buses and park shuttles connect the scenic area to town
transport.ferry: None scheduled — bamboo rafting on the Nine-Bend River is recreational, not a transport link
transport.car: A car or driver is useful for reaching Xiamei Village and outlying tea plantations; the scenic area's interior is closed to private cars, shuttle only

airport.name: Wuyishan Airport
airport.distance: ~8 km (15-20 min) from Wuyishan city center
airport.transport: Taxi ~$8-10 fare into town; Didi or hotel pickup recommended given limited airport shuttle service

net.m: Solid 4G in town and along the high-speed rail corridor; weaker inside the scenic area's deeper trails
net.w: Free wifi in hotels and tea houses in town
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.fwn: VPN needed for Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook — install before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM in Fuzhou or Xiamen before heading to Wuyishan; local shops have limited tourist SIM stock

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

tagline: Dai temples, elephant-crossed jungles, and Mekong sunsets in China's tropical southern frontier.
langs: Hani, Jinuo, Bulang, and other minority languages
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international-brand hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for nearly everything — set up mobile payment before arrival

taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard in town, but drivers to outlying villages or the botanical garden usually quote a flat round-trip fare

emergency.medical: 120 (ambulance); Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture People's Hospital in Jinghong
emergency.note: Heat exhaustion and river-current incidents are the most common tourist emergencies; English support is limited outside major hotels

religion: Han Chinese majority nonreligious or Mahayana Buddhist/Taoist
visit: tea trekking near the Six Great Tea Mountains
walk: Jinghong's riverside core and night-market streets are pleasant on foot, but most major sights — the botanical garden, elephant valley, Dai villages — require a car, bus, or Didi ride out of town

safety.safety: Very safe, relaxed resort-town atmosphere popular with solo Chinese travelers
safety.crime: Low — biggest risks are heat/sun exposure, river currents, and tourist-market overcharging

hood_landmark.Jinghong City Center: Mekong River promenade and Peacock Lake
hood_landmark.Gaozhuang Night Market: Gaozhuang International Trade City night market

hood_desc: The Mekong-side core of wide boulevards and palm trees, with the riverside promenade, prefecture museum, and Peacock Lake nearby.
Home to Manting Park's royal Dai gardens and Buddhist temples, a green, templed pocket just east of downtown.
Jinghong's after-dark hub of skewer stalls, fruit vendors, and bars, busiest after sunset when the heat breaks.
A cluster of traditional Dai stilt-house villages and the Dai Minority Garden theme park, downstream along the Mekong.
Home to the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, a riverbend peninsula of rainforest about an hour from the city.

transit.sys: City buses plus long-distance minibuses to Dai villages and Menglun
transit.note: No metro; Didi ride-hailing covers the city well, but rural villages and gardens need buses or a hired driver

transport.air: Xishuangbanna Gasa International Airport (JHG), ~6 km from downtown Jinghong, with flights to Kunming, other major Chinese cities, and a handful of Southeast Asia routes
transport.train: Xishuangbanna (Jinghong) railway station on the China–Laos Railway — direct high-speed service to Kunming (~3.5 hrs) and onward to Vientiane, Laos
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Jinghong to Kunming (~8-10 hrs by road) and cross-border routes toward Laos and Myanmar
transport.ferry: Seasonal Mekong River cargo/passenger boats run toward Laos, though scheduled tourist ferry service is limited
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired driver is useful for reaching Dai villages, tea mountains, and the botanical garden, which are spread across the prefecture

airport.name: Xishuangbanna Gasa International Airport
airport.transport: Taxi ~$5-8 metered fare into town; airport shuttle bus to the city center also available

net.m: Good 4G/5G in Jinghong city; coverage thins out in remote Dai villages and tea-mountain areas
net.w: Free wifi at hotels and cafes in the city center
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.fwn: VPN required for Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and most Western apps
net.ap: SIM/eSIM is easiest to buy in Kunming before flying or training in; Jinghong airport has a China Mobile counter

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

tagline: China's only island-built city — a Buddhist sea kingdom, nine sand beaches, and 1,390 islands scattered across the East China Sea
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international-standard hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay dominate nearly every transaction — set up mobile payment before arrival and carry some cash as backup.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard within Dinghai and Putuo; inter-island trips are usually flat-rate — agree the price before boarding

emergency.note: Fire is 119. English support is minimal outside major hotels — have your hotel call for you in an emergency.

religion: Buddhism (Mt. Putuo is one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains, drawing pilgrims islandwide)
visit: Guanyin statue at Nanhai (South China Sea Guanyin)
Zhujiajian Island's Dajiao and Nanguo Bay beaches
walk: Dinghai Old Town and the Mt. Putuo pilgrim paths are compact and walkable; the archipelago overall requires ferries and buses to move between islands, so plan around boat schedules rather than expecting to walk between sights.

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers; a popular domestic pilgrimage and beach destination with low crime
safety.crime: Minimal — occasional overcharging by unlicensed ferry touts or souvenir vendors near Mt. Putuo's temples is the main annoyance

hood_landmark.Dinghai Old Town: Zhoushan Museum and the Qing-dynasty lanes
hood_landmark.Mt. Putuo (Putuoshan): Nanhai Guanyin statue and Puji Temple
hood_landmark.Shenjiamen (Putuo District): Shenjiamen fishing port and seafood market
hood_landmark.Taohua Island: Taohua Peak lighthouse and film-location coves

hood_desc: The archipelago's historic administrative seat — a walkable grid of Qing-dynasty stone lanes, canal bridges, and the city museum, with the widest choice of everyday hotels and restaurants.

A dedicated pilgrimage island reached by a short ferry, packed with Buddhist temples, monasteries, and quiet beaches — overnight stays are in temple guesthouses or hillside hotels rather than a town center.
A resort island famous for its long sand beaches and seafood restaurants, popular with mainland Chinese beachgoers in summer and connected to the mainland by bridge.
Zhoushan's largest fishing port and commercial fleet base, with a lively seafood market and ferry terminals to the outer islands.
A quieter, less-developed island known for dramatic sea cliffs and as a filming location for classic Chinese cinema, reached by ferry from Shenjiamen.

transit.sys: City buses on the main islands plus inter-island ferries (the primary way to travel between Zhoushan's islands)
transit.map: Use Amap (Gaode) or Baidu Maps — not on Google Maps
transit.note: Bridges now connect the main island cluster (Dinghai, Zhujiajian) but Mt. Putuo and Taohua remain ferry-only, so budget extra time around boat schedules

transport.air: Zhoushan Putuoshan Airport (HSN) on Zhujiajian Island has domestic flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou and other major cities
transport.train: No direct rail to the islands; nearest high-speed rail is Ningbo, connected onward by a 1.5-2 hour bus/bridge crossing
transport.bus: Long-distance buses and bridge crossings connect Zhoushan to Ningbo, Shanghai and Hangzhou via the Zhoushan Cross-Sea Bridge
transport.ferry: Frequent passenger ferries link Dinghai, Mt. Putuo, Zhujiajian, Shenjiamen and the outer islands — the essential way to island-hop
transport.car: Self-driving works well for the bridge-linked main islands (Dinghai to Zhujiajian); Mt. Putuo and Taohua require leaving the car and taking a ferry

airport.name: Zhoushan Putuoshan Airport
airport.distance: On Zhujiajian Island, ~45 min by bridge/ferry combo to Dinghai
airport.transport: Airport shuttle bus to Dinghai and Shenjiamen; taxi/Didi also available

net.m: Good 4G/5G in Dinghai, Zhujiajian and Shenjiamen; signal weakens on Mt. Putuo's forested trails and remote outer islands
net.w: Free wifi common in hotels and cafes on the main islands
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.gb: ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM
net.fwn: The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM in Shanghai, Hangzhou or Ningbo before heading to the islands; local stock is limited

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

pop: ~740,000 urban (Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture seat; prefecture-wide ~4 million)
tagline: China's Grand Canyon, carved through Tujia and Miao mountain country in southwestern Hubei
langs: Tujia and Miao languages (mostly ceremonial/minority use)
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside a few international-standard hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for nearly everything — set up mobile payment before arrival and keep some cash as backup.

taxi.color: mixed liveries, mostly green and white sedans
taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard in town; trips to the Grand Canyon or Tenglong Cave scenic areas are usually flat-rate — agree the price upfront

emergency.note: Fire is 119. English support is minimal — hotel staff can help translate in an emergency.

religion: Folk religion and ancestor veneration (Tujia and Miao traditions)
visit: Enshi Grand Canyon: Yunlong Ground Fissure and the glass skywalk
Tenglong Cave, one of China's largest karst caves
Tujia ethnic dance performance inside the cave
Yumu Village traditional Tujia stilt houses
walk: Downtown Enshi is compact and walkable, but the Grand Canyon, Tenglong Cave and Qingjiang rafting sites are all outside town and require a bus, tour van, or taxi/Didi ride — expect significant stair-climbing and cliffside walkways at the canyon itself.

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers; a growing domestic eco-tourism destination with low crime
safety.crime: Minimal — the main risks are trail-related (steep steps, cliffside walkways) rather than crime

hood_landmark.Enshi City Center: Enshi State Central Hospital area and the pedestrian shopping street
hood_landmark.Qingjiang Chuangtan: The 48-rapid rafting course on the Qing River

hood_desc: The functional prefecture capital with the bus stations, hospitals, and everyday hotels and restaurants — the practical base for exploring the surrounding canyon country.
A dramatic limestone gorge about an hour from downtown, with a glass-floored skywalk and cliffside trails above the Yunlong ground fissure.
Home to one of China's largest karst cave systems, with an underground river and nightly Tujia cultural performances inside the cavern.
A rafting stretch of the Qing River known for 48 rapids, popular with domestic adventure tourists in summer.
A preserved Tujia minority village of traditional wooden stilt houses, offering a quieter look at the region's ethnic heritage.

transit.sys: City buses plus scenic-area shuttle buses
transit.note: Tour buses and shuttles run from downtown to the Grand Canyon and Tenglong Cave; a private driver or Didi is the easiest way to combine multiple sites in a day

transport.air: Enshi Xujiaping Airport (ENH), ~5 km from downtown, with domestic flights to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Xi'an and other major cities
transport.train: Enshi railway station on the Yichang-Wanzhou line connects to Wuhan (~4-5 hrs) and Chongqing
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect Enshi to Wuhan, Chongqing, and Zhangjiajie; local buses and scenic shuttles serve the canyon and cave
transport.ferry: None — Enshi is inland mountain terrain with no scheduled passenger ferry service
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired driver is useful for combining the Grand Canyon, Tenglong Cave, and Yumu Village in one trip; mountain roads are winding but well paved to the main sites

airport.name: Enshi Xujiaping Airport
airport.transport: Airport shuttle bus to the city center; taxi/Didi also available

net.m: Good 4G in downtown Enshi and along main roads; patchy inside the canyon and cave scenic areas
net.w: Free wifi in most hotels and cafes
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.gb: ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM
net.fwn: The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM in Wuhan or another major hub before traveling to Enshi; local stock is limited

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; rarely a service charge outside upscale hotel restaurants

tagline: China's busiest land port, where Russian onion domes, Mongolian grasslands, and a 30-meter Matryoshka doll collide
card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international-standard hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay dominate — set up mobile payment before arrival. Russian rubles are informally accepted in some border-trade shops but yuan is standard.

taxi.color: mixed liveries, mostly red and white sedans
taxi.fareNote: Meters are standard in town; trips to Hulun Lake or the border-crossing tourist area are usually flat-rate — agree the price upfront

emergency.note: Fire is 119. English support is minimal — Russian is more commonly understood than English due to cross-border trade.

religion: small Russian Orthodox and Christian minority
visit: Matryoshka Square and the giant nesting-doll landmarks
Russian-style architecture along the main boulevards
night light show on Manzhouli's landmark buildings
Hulun Lake (Dalai Nur) scenic area and grassland drive
birdwatching (swans, cranes, wild ducks) on the lakeshore
Russian goods market for border-trade shopping
walk: Central Manzhouli's main boulevards (Erdaojie area) are walkable and lined with distinctive Russian-influenced architecture; Hulun Lake and the border crossing require a taxi, Didi, or tour bus.

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers; a well-policed border-trade city with low crime
safety.crime: Minimal — standard caution around border-market bargaining and currency exchange is enough

hood_landmark.Central Manzhouli (Erdaojie): Matryoshka Square and the Russian-style boulevard architecture
hood_landmark.Hulun Lake (Dalai Nur) Area: Hulun Lake's grassland shoreline and birdwatching spots
hood_landmark.Xingfu (Happiness) District: Local residential streets and everyday markets

hood_desc: The city's showpiece core, where candy-colored Russian-revival buildings, the giant Matryoshka doll landmarks, and nightly illuminated light shows draw domestic tourists after dark.
The working border-crossing zone where Chinese and Russian traders exchange goods, with markets selling Russian chocolate, vodka, and souvenirs alongside customs facilities.
A grassland lake area about 45 minutes from downtown, popular for birdwatching, horseback riding, and Mongolian-style yurt stays in summer.
The historic railway quarter built during the Russian-administered Chinese Eastern Railway era, with the city's oldest surviving station architecture.
A quieter residential district away from the tourist core, with everyday shops and local eateries for a look at ordinary Manzhouli life.

transit.sys: City buses cover the compact downtown core
transit.note: Manzhouli's core is small and walkable; buses and Didi cover Hulun Lake and the border zone

transport.air: Manzhouli Xijiao International Airport (NZH), ~12 km from downtown, with domestic flights to Beijing, Hohhot, Harbin and other cities
transport.train: Manzhouli railway station, a historic stop on the Chinese Eastern Railway, connects to Harbin, Beijing, and cross-border toward Zabaykalsk, Russia
transport.bus: Long-distance buses and cross-border coaches connect Manzhouli to Hailar and, via the border crossing, to Zabaykalsk, Russia
transport.ferry: None — Manzhouli is a landlocked border city with no passenger ferry service
transport.car: Self-driving or a hired car is useful for reaching Hulun Lake and the surrounding grasslands; Highway 301 links Manzhouli to Hailar and the wider Hulunbuir region

airport.name: Manzhouli Xijiao International Airport
airport.transport: Airport shuttle bus to the city center; taxi/Didi also available

net.m: Good 4G in downtown Manzhouli; weaker out on the Hulun Lake grasslands
net.w: Free wifi common in hotels and cafes downtown
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.gb: ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM
net.fwn: The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM in Beijing or Harbin before traveling to Manzhouli; local stock is limited

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; rarely a service charge outside upscale hotel restaurants

tagline: A belle-époque spa town on the edge of the Black Forest, where thermal baths and a grand casino have drawn European royalty for two centuries
card: Contactless and card payment are the norm at hotels, restaurants, and the casino; small cafes, market stalls, and some spa facilities may prefer cash, so carry a little euros.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; airport transfers to Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden Airport or Stuttgart are usually flat-rate — confirm before boarding

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number and reaches English-speaking dispatchers in most cases

visit: Old Town lanes and the Stiftskirche
Merkur mountain funicular and hiking trails
Baden-Baden Racecourse (Iffezheim) if timed with a race meeting
walk: The compact spa-town core between the Kurhaus, casino, and Lichtentaler Allee is entirely walkable and pedestrian-friendly; the Old Town's hillside lanes involve some gentle climbing, and Merkur mountain is reached by a short funicular rather than on foot.

safety.safety: Very safe; Baden-Baden is a genteel resort town with very low crime and is comfortable for solo travelers at any hour
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; the main caution is standard care with valuables in busy tourist areas like the casino and spa lockers

hood_landmark.Altstadt (Old Town): Stiftskirche and the New Castle hillside
hood_landmark.Lichtental: Lichtentaler Allee promenade and Kloster Lichtenthal abbey
hood_landmark.Weststadt / Rebland: Vineyard slopes toward the Rhine valley

hood_desc: The elegant heart of the spa town, centered on the Kurhaus, casino, and grand 19th-century hotels — the natural base for most visitors and home to the thermal baths.
The hillside medieval core above the spa quarter, with narrow lanes, the Stiftskirche, and the New Castle offering panoramic views over the town.
A quiet, leafy district along the Lichtentaler Allee promenade, anchored by the historic Cistercian abbey and rose gardens — a peaceful, residential contrast to the casino district.
The wine-growing fringe toward the Rhine valley, dotted with vineyards and a more local, less touristy pace.
A hilltop village a short drive or hike above town, known for its ruined castle and sweeping Black Forest views.

transit.pay: Contactless card, KVV app, or cash on board; day tickets available
transit.map: Route maps at kvv.de and posted at bus stops
transit.note: The compact center is easily walkable; buses mainly serve outlying districts like Ebersteinburg and Rebland

transport.air: Baden-Baden Karlsruhe Airport (FKB), ~10 km away, with flights on Ryanair and others to European cities; Stuttgart Airport (STR) is a larger alternative about 1 hour away
transport.train: Baden-Baden station has ICE high-speed connections to Frankfurt (~1.5 hrs), Basel, and Karlsruhe; the station is about 15 minutes from the town center by bus or taxi
transport.bus: FlixBus and regional coaches connect Baden-Baden to Stuttgart, Karlsruhe, and Strasbourg
transport.ferry: None — Baden-Baden is inland with no ferry service
transport.car: Easily reached via the A5 autobahn; parking in the compact center is limited, so many hotels offer valet or garage parking

airport.name: Baden-Baden Karlsruhe Airport
airport.transport: Airport shuttle bus timed to flights; taxi transfer roughly €25-35

net.m: Excellent 4G/5G coverage throughout Baden-Baden and the surrounding Black Forest foothills
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels, cafes, and the Kurhaus
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in cafes and public spaces in the town center
net.ap: EU roaming covers most European visitors; a prepaid German SIM or eSIM is easy to buy at the airport or a phone shop for others

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up or a small tip for spa attendants and hotel staff is appreciated
tip.r: 5-10% is customary if service isn't already included — hand the tip directly to the server rather than leaving it on the table

tagline: A UNESCO-listed island town of half-timbered houses, smoked beer, and a cathedral rising over the River Regnitz
card: Contactless and card payment are widely accepted at hotels, restaurants, and shops; some traditional beer cellars and market stalls in the Altstadt prefer cash, so carry a little euros.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; the Altstadt's pedestrian zones mean taxis often drop off at the edge of the historic core

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number and typically reaches English-speaking dispatchers

visit: Altes Rathaus (Old Town Hall) on its river-island bridge
Bamberg Cathedral (Bamberger Dom) and the Bamberg Rider statue
Neue Residenz palace and Rose Garden viewpoint
Schlenkerla and other historic Rauchbier (smoked beer) taverns on a self-guided brewery crawl
walk: Extremely walkable — the compact UNESCO-listed island town center can be crossed end to end in about 20 minutes, with cobblestone lanes linking the Altes Rathaus, cathedral hill, and Little Venice; a bit of climbing is required for the cathedral and Altenburg Castle viewpoints.

safety.safety: Very safe; Bamberg is a low-crime university and heritage town comfortable for solo travelers at any hour
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; standard caution applies around the train station and busy beer-festival crowds (e.g., Sandkerwa in August)

hood_desc: The postcard core of Bamberg, built on an island in the River Regnitz, with the iconic Altes Rathaus straddling two bridges and the pastel fishermen's houses of Little Venice along the water.
The ecclesiastical high point of the city, crowned by the four-towered cathedral and the Prince-Bishops' Neue Residenz, with sweeping rooftop views from the Rose Garden.
A bohemian, student-favored quarter across the river from the Altstadt, home to Bamberg's smoke-beer breweries and a livelier bar and cafe scene.
A UNESCO-protected market-gardening district where family plots still supply the city's produce, offering a quieter, greener side of Bamberg.
The practical gateway near the train station, with everyday shops and budget-friendly hotels a short walk from the historic core.

transit.pay: Contactless card, VGN app, or cash on board; day tickets available
transit.map: Route maps at stadtwerke-bamberg.de and posted at bus stops
transit.note: The Altstadt is fully walkable; buses mainly serve outlying residential areas and the train station

transport.air: Nearest major airport is Nuremberg (NUE), about 60 km / 50 minutes by car or train; Frankfurt is a larger international option about 2.5 hours away
transport.train: Bamberg Hauptbahnhof has frequent regional and ICE connections to Nuremberg (~40 min), Würzburg, Leipzig, and Berlin
transport.bus: FlixBus and regional coaches connect Bamberg to Nuremberg, Munich, and other Bavarian cities
transport.ferry: None — Bamberg is inland with no scheduled passenger ferry, though the Main-Danube Canal passes nearby
transport.car: Reachable via the A73 autobahn; the Altstadt is largely pedestrianized, so park at the edge and walk in

airport.name: Nuremberg Airport
airport.distance: ~60 km (50 min by car or train)
airport.transport: Direct train connections via Nuremberg Hauptbahnhof; taxi transfer roughly €80-100

net.m: Excellent 4G/5G coverage throughout Bamberg and the surrounding Franconia region
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels, cafes, and many public squares
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in cafes and the Altstadt's public spaces
net.ap: EU roaming covers most European visitors; a prepaid German SIM or eSIM is easy to buy at Nuremberg Airport or a phone shop

tagline: The intellectual capital of German Classicism, where Goethe and Schiller once walked and the Bauhaus was born
langs: English (widely spoken in tourist and museum areas)
card: Contactless and card payment are standard at hotels, restaurants, and museums; small cafes and the weekly market may prefer cash, so carry a little euros.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; the compact Altstadt is largely pedestrian, so taxis drop off at the edge of the historic core

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number and typically reaches English-speaking dispatchers

religion: Unaffiliated/none ~65% (Thuringia is one of Germany's least religious regions)
visit: Duchess Anna Amalia Library's Rococo Hall
Park an der Ilm landscaped park
Weimar's historic cemetery and the Fürstengruft royal crypt
Buchenwald Memorial (former concentration camp, a somber but historically essential half-day visit)
walk: Highly walkable — the compact Altstadt links Goethe's House, Schiller's House, Theaterplatz, and the Anna Amalia Library within a 15-20 minute walk; Park an der Ilm and Belvedere require a bit more walking or a short bus ride, and Buchenwald is reached by bus or car outside town.

safety.safety: Very safe; Weimar is a low-crime university and heritage town comfortable for solo travelers at any hour
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; standard caution applies in crowded museum queues and around the train station

hood_landmark.Park an der Ilm: Goethe's Garden House in the landscaped park
hood_landmark.Weimar-West: Modernist residential district (less touristy, everyday Weimar)

hood_desc: The compact historic core packed with Goethe- and Schiller-era landmarks, the Anna Amalia Library, and Theaterplatz — the obvious base for exploring Weimar Classicism on foot.
A sweeping English-style landscaped park along the River Ilm, dotted with follies, Goethe's rustic Garden House, and quiet riverside paths just steps from the Altstadt.
The modern counterpart to Weimar's classical heritage, centered on the Bauhaus Museum and sites tied to the founding of the influential 20th-century design movement.
A quieter residential district west of the center, offering a look at everyday, non-touristy Weimar and more budget-friendly lodging.
The wooded hilltop north of town holding the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial — a solemn, historically vital half-day visit reached by bus.

transit.pay: Contactless card, VMT app, or cash on board; day tickets available
transit.map: Route maps at swg-weimar.de and posted at bus stops
transit.note: The Altstadt is fully walkable; buses are mainly useful for Buchenwald, Belvedere, and outlying residential districts

transport.air: Nearest airports are Erfurt-Weimar (ERF), about 20 km / 25 minutes away with limited flights, and Leipzig/Halle (LEJ), a larger option about 1.5 hours away
transport.train: Weimar Hauptbahnhof has frequent regional and ICE connections to Erfurt (~15 min), Leipzig, and Frankfurt
transport.bus: FlixBus and regional coaches connect Weimar to Erfurt, Leipzig, and other German cities; local buses serve Buchenwald and outlying sites
transport.ferry: None — Weimar is inland with no ferry service
transport.car: Reachable via the A4 autobahn; the Altstadt is largely pedestrianized, so park at the edge and walk in

airport.name: Erfurt-Weimar Airport
airport.transport: Taxi transfer roughly €35-45; regional train via Erfurt Hauptbahnhof is a cheaper alternative

net.ap: EU roaming covers most European visitors; a prepaid German SIM or eSIM is easy to buy at Leipzig/Halle Airport or a phone shop
